title: The Compound Palm Bay — What Buyers Should Know About Units 51, 52 & 53 in 2026
content:
The Compound — 2,492 acres of platted but underdeveloped land in southwest Palm Bay, finally on the city's redevelopment radar.

For 50 years, Port Malabar Units 51, 52, and 53 — known locally as "The Compound" — have sat with roads but no utilities. In 2024 and 2025 that finally started to change. If you are a buyer, builder, or patient investor, this is the area you should understand before everyone else does.

Important: Our Compound lots in Units 51, 52, and 53 are sold only as one whole package. They are not sold one lot at a time. Most Compound lots are not buildable on their own today.

The Short Version

I have been selling land in Palm Bay since 2003. I have been watching the compound that entire time, and I have never seen this much real activity around it. EPA studies, a $1.5 million brownfields grant, a city redevelopment action plan, and a proposed "Port Malabar Industrial" designation are all moving forward at once.

This is still a long-horizon situation. Here is what is actually happening and what it means for buyers.

Where The Compound Actually Sits

One of the most underappreciated facts about the compound is its location. It is not in the middle of nowhere. It sits inside the city limits of Palm Bay — the largest city in Brevard County — between Orlando and the Space Coast.

The Compound sits inside Palm Bay city limits, minutes from I-95, between Orlando and the Space Coast between Orlando and the Space Coast.

  • ~10 minutes to Interstate 95
  • ~45 minutes to Orlando International Airport
  • ~45 minutes to Kennedy Space Center / Cape Canaveral
  • Inside city limits of Palm Bay (130,000+ residents, Brevard County's largest city)

It is one of the largest blocks of mostly undeveloped land inside a Brevard County city.

What Is Actually Happening — Verified, 2024–2026

This is not speculation. Each of these is documented public record:

The City of Palm Bay's Compound Redevelopment Action Plan — the first official strategic document for the area in 50 years.

1. EPA Land Revitalization Study (Unit 53)

The City of Palm Bay secured a $100,000 technical assistance grant from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, specifically focused on Port Malabar Unit 53. The output is a formal action plan to encourage economic development in the area. The study has been delivered — and the public-facing "Compound Redevelopment Action Plan" is the result.

2. $1.5 Million Brownfields Assessment Grant

The compound is named as a priority site in a $1.5 million brownfields assessment grant awarded to the Resilient Corridors Coalition. Brownfields funding pays for the environmental and land-use assessments that have to happen before private development can move forward at scale. In plain English: this money clears the runway.

3. Port Malabar Industrial Designation (Proposed)

The northern section of the compound has been formally studied for a future "Port Malabar Industrial" land-use designation. The city has not yet adopted the rezoning, but the planning work is done. Any future land use change is up to the City of Palm Bay and is not guaranteed.

4. City-Owned Parcels Inside The Compound

The City of Palm Bay itself owns multiple parcels inside the compound boundary. Cities do not commit staff time, planning dollars, and EPA partnerships to areas they intend to leave alone. The city has skin in the game.

Parcel-level view of the entire Compound — yellow outlines are individual lots; red outlines are city-owned parcels inside the boundary.

5. A Gateway Vision — Port Malabar Business Park

The redevelopment action plan includes a specific gateway concept: a branded business-park entry at the main access point, anchoring the future identity of the area. This is the kind of detail that signals the city is thinking about the compound as a real district — not just a problem to be inherited.

A proposed gateway monument from the city's redevelopment action plan — the kind of branding cities only invest in when they expect a district to materialize.

What This Means for Buyers

For decades the Compound drew little interest because it has roads but no utilities. The city's action plan, the EPA study, and the brownfields grant are the first formal steps toward changing that. They are studies and plans, not funded construction.

Honest disclosure: Today, most Compound lots have no city water, no city sewer, and no power at the lot line. Most are not buildable on their own today. Timelines are unknown and future values are not guaranteed.

How Our Compound Lots Are Sold

Our Compound lots in Units 51, 52, and 53 are sold only as one whole package. We do not sell them one lot at a time. The package fits developers, builders, and long-horizon land investors who can plan at a large scale.

Before any purchase, the parcels should be checked with Brevard County GIS, the Brevard County Property Appraiser, and the City of Palm Bay Land Development Division. I can help pull that information.

Risk — Stated Plainly

  • The timeline is uncertain. Studies and grants are real, but adopted construction plans with funded timelines are not yet in place.
  • When utilities do arrive, owners will likely be assessed for their share, typically spread over 10–20 years on the property tax bill.
  • Insurance, ongoing taxes, and code-enforcement maintenance (mowing requirements) are the owner's responsibility from day one.

The Bottom Line

The Compound is getting more attention from the City of Palm Bay than at any time in its 50-year history. That is a fact about planning activity, not a promise about prices. faqs.q: Is The Compound actually buildable today?
faqs.a: Most of The Compound has no water, sewer, or power today, and most lots are not buildable on their own. A small number of homes have been built using well, septic, and extended power near existing infrastructure. Always verify any specific parcel.

faqs.q: Can I buy just one Compound lot?
faqs.a: No. Our Compound lots in Units 51, 52, and 53 are sold only as one whole package. They are not sold one by one.

faqs.q: How much does the Compound package cost?
faqs.a: Pricing for the whole package is discussed directly. Call 321-333-7230.

faqs.q: Will owners get an assessment when utilities arrive?
faqs.a: When city utilities arrive, property owners in the assessment area will likely be billed proportionally. That cost is typically spread over 10–20 years on the property tax bill.

faqs.q: What about the proposed Port Malabar Industrial designation?
faqs.a: The northern Compound area has been formally studied for industrial land use. No rezoning has been adopted yet. Any future change is up to the City of Palm Bay and is not guaranteed.
